phonemes.desc: Voiceless glottal fricative [h], as in English 'hall'; Old Norse initial h is fully sounded.
Short close-mid front [e], held brief — the short vowel of the verb heljan, not a long é.
Single clear alveolar lateral [l]; the manuscripts write one l, and the name keeps it light.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HEL' — one crisp syllable: a fully sounded h, a short bright 'e' as in 'get', a single clean l. The English word 'hell' is the name's own descendant and nearly its own pronunciation.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Hel — the goddess and the realm; the common noun hel also means the grave, death.

kin.label: Gothic
kin.form: halja — the word Ulfilas's fourth-century Bible uses for the underworld, the oldest Germanic attestation of the name.

kin.label: Old English / Old High German
kin.form: helle / hella — the same word as a place-name for the dead; England and the continent kept the realm without the goddess.

kin.label: Proto-Germanic
kin.form: *haljō, from *helan / *heljan 'to conceal, to cover' — the hidden thing, and the one who hides.

pronunciation.note: Hel is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no vowel length for the restoration to rescue. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The goddess's gravity vastly outruns her name's orthography; three letters carry the whole underworld.

domains.title: Death, Underworld, Souls
domains.subtitle: The Hidden One Who Keeps the Unheroic Dead
domains.lead: Hel is the daughter of Loki and Angrboða whom Óðinn cast down into Niflheimr and set over the dead: half blue-black and half the colour of living flesh, she rules Éljúðnir, where those who die of sickness and old age — the vast, unburned majority of humankind — are sent to her keeping.

cards.name: Éljúðnir
cards.desc: Her hall, 'Sprayed with Snowstorms', behind high walls and great gates — the dwelling Snorri names as the terminus of every quiet death.

cards.name: Hungr and Sultr
cards.desc: Her dish is Hunger, her knife Famine: the furniture of her table names the slow wasting she presides over.

cards.name: Fallanda Forað
cards.desc: 'Plunging to Destruction' — the threshold of her bedchamber, one of the named fittings of the hall in Gylfaginning's grim inventory.

cards.name: The Half-Living Face
cards.desc: Half blue-black, half the colour of flesh — 'easily recognized', Snorri says, downcast and fierce: the visible seam between the quick and the dead.

symbols.name: The half-blue, half-flesh face
symbols.meaning: The two states of being worn on one head — life and corruption divided by a single line

symbols.name: Éljúðnir
symbols.meaning: The hall of the dead who were not burned in battle — architecture for the ordinary ending

symbols.name: Hungr the dish and Sultr the knife
symbols.meaning: Hunger and famine as table-service — the realm named out of what it takes away

symbols.name: Fallanda Forað and Kǫr
symbols.meaning: The plunging threshold and the sick-bed, hung with Blíkjanda Bǫl, 'Gleaming Bale' — the dead received as the sick received to bed

symbols.name: Ganglati and Ganglǫt
symbols.meaning: Her serving-man and serving-maid, both named for the slow walk — time in Hel moves at a dying pace

mythology.lead: Hel acts rarely and presides always. The corpus gives her one origin, one judgment, and a standing geography — and in exchange she receives nearly everyone. The myths agree that the gods could not kill her; they could only give her what they most wanted hidden, and make her keeper of it forever.

myths.title: The Casting Down
myths.text:
Loki got three children on the giantess Angrboða in Jötunheimr: the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jǫrmungandr, and Hel. When the gods learned that this brood was being raised, and read in the prophecies that great harm would come of them, Óðinn sent for the children and disposed of each: the serpent he threw into the deep sea that circles all lands, the wolf the Æsir kept to bind, and Hel he cast down into Niflheimr. There he gave her authority over nine worlds, that she should apportion all dwellings among those sent to her — and those are the sickness-dead and the age-dead.

Snorri then gives the strangest inventory in the Edda. Her hall is called Éljúðnir; her dish Hungr, Hunger; her knife Sultr, Famine; her serving-man Ganglati and her serving-maid Ganglǫt, the slow-walking pair; the threshold she steps over is Fallanda Forað, Plunging to Destruction; her bed is Kǫr, the sick-bed, and its hangings Blíkjanda Bǫl, Gleaming Bale. And of Hel herself: she is half blue-black and half the colour of living flesh, and therefore easily recognized — rather downcast and fierce of countenance. The goddess of death is furnished out of the slow deaths she rules: her household is a ward, and she is its matron with a corpse's half-face.

myths.title: The Weeping Condition
myths.text:
When Baldr lay dead and Hermóðr the Bold had ridden nine nights down the dark road, he came to Helgrindr, the barred gate, spurred Sleipnir, and leapt it unopened. In the hall he found Baldr seated in the high seat — the most honoured of the dead already given Hel's highest place — and he stayed the night. In the morning he asked Hel to let Baldr ride home with him, and told her how great the weeping was among the Æsir.

Hel's answer is her only speech in the corpus, and the whole ending of the world turns on it: she would test whether Baldr was as beloved as was said. If all things in the world, living and lifeless, weep for him, he shall go back to the Æsir — but he shall stay with Hel if anything speaks against it or refuses to weep. Everything wept: men and beasts, earth and stones, trees and metals. Only the giantess Þökk in her cave wept dry tears: 'Let Hel hold what she has.' The sentence is usually read as Loki's cruelty. It is also, word for word, Hel's own charter: she holds what she has. No one has ever gotten it back from her by force.

myths.title: The Geography of the Hidden
myths.text:
The Poetic Edda keeps her realm on the map rather than on the stage. When Óðinn, disguised, wagers his head against the giant Vafþrúðnir's wisdom, his proof that he has travelled farther than any god is this: 'Nine worlds I came through, down below Niflhel; thither men die out of Hel.' The line folds the dead downward through layers — there is a Hel, and there is something below Hel, a death beneath death for those already dead.

Grímnismál plants the same region in the world-tree's architecture: three roots hold Yggdrasill, and Hel dwells beneath one of them, while men dwell beneath another and the frost-giants beneath the third. The dead are not elsewhere; they are under the same tree, at another root. The hidden one is hidden in the most literal way the Norse cosmos allows — covered by the world's own structure.

myths.title: The Strewn Benches
myths.text:
Before Baldr ever falls, Óðinn saddles Sleipnir and rides down the same road his son Hermóðr will ride after, to the grave of a völva east of Hel's gate. He raises her with spells and demands to know for whom the realm below is dressed. She answers unwilling: the benches are strewn with arm-rings, the dais fairly decked, the mead brewed, the shields overspread — for Baldr. The hope of the gods departs.

The poem's glimpse inside the hall is the other side of Gylfaginning's inventory of hunger and slow walking: Hel's house is also a hall of honour, strewn and shining like Valhǫll for the guest it expects. The deadliest hospitality in the Edda is prepared in advance, and it is beautiful. Baldr will sit in that high seat within the year.

lore.syncretism: The oldest syncretism is the one the sources perform on themselves: Saxo Grammaticus, writing Latin for a Danish court, cannot say 'Hel' and so writes Proserpina — in Gesta Danorum Book 1 the goddess appears to Balderus in a dream as Proserpina, promising the dead man her embraces, the interpretatio latina folded directly into the plot. The Greek comparison runs deeper than the name-swap suggests: like Hades, Hel is both a person and a place, and the Old Norse word does the same double duty — one goes til Heljar, to Hel, as one goes to Hades. Jacob Grimm projected the goddess backward onto the continent as *Halja, citing the Gothic and Old High German words; current scholarship (Simek, Lindow) is cooler, noting that the continental languages attest the realm but never the ruler, and that the goddess may be a Scandinavian personification of an older common noun — the hidden place given a face. The largest syncretism is the one history performed without asking: Christianity took the word itself and made it 'hell', the punitive fire of the damned, recolouring the goddess's quiet hall of the sick-dead into the most feared address in the language. Her name survived by being emptied of her.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hel's afterlife is the English language's own: every speaker of English, German, or the Scandinavian tongues still pronounces her name every time they say hell — the commonest relic any Norse deity has left behind, carried out of the temple and into the swear-word. The word's journey is her biography in reverse: the goddess faded, the place-name endured, and the place darkened from a hall of the age-dead into a prison of fire. Modern reception has restored the person, if not the theology: she returns in Wagnerian and Victorian mythography, in Neil Gaiman's retellings, and most visibly in Marvel's Hela, whose half-shadowed iconography reaches back past the comics to Snorri's two-coloured face. Modern Heathenry keeps her as the keeper of the ordinary ancestors — the goddess for everyone who will not die in battle, which is to say, for nearly everyone.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hel is what the gods do with what they cannot destroy. Óðinn cannot kill Loki's daughter — the prophecies forbid the thought — so he hides her, and the hiding is so thorough that it becomes an office: the concealed one becomes the keeper of everyone else the world conceals. Her name says it plainly: the hidden one, from the verb for covering over. Every grave is a small act of heljan. And her charter is more honest than Valhǫll's: Óðinn's hall takes the spectacular few, the spear-marked and the chosen; Hel takes the rest — the sick, the old, the children, the farmers in their beds — which is to say she receives, in the end, almost the whole of humankind, and keeps it behind a gate no god has ever forced. 'Let Hel hold what she has' was meant as a curse. It is also simply the truth of things, and the Edda knew it: everything that dies quietly is already hers, and she has never once given it back.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Hel — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᛁᛚ (h-i-l, the ᛁ-rune covering e, as the Viking-Age row does not distinguish the front vowels). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: hel.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Vafþrúðnismál 43 (the nine worlds below Niflhel; men dying out of Hel), Grímnismál 31 (Hel dwelling beneath one root of Yggdrasill), and Baldrs draumar (the benches strewn and the mead brewed for Baldr)

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 34 (Loki's children; Hel cast into Niflheimr; the hall Éljúðnir and its named fittings; her half-blue appearance) and 49 (Hermóðr's errand and the weeping condition)
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 1 (Proserpina's promise to Balderus; Hading's journey under the earth), trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. hel (death, the grave, the goddess) and heljan
Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. Hel, hel

Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology; Orchard, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend; Lindow, Norse Mythology: A Guide — s.v. Hel (the etymology, the personification debate, and the realm-versus-ruler problem)

lore.archaeology: Hel is a textual figure: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no Scandinavian place-name can be securely tied to her cult — a silence she shares with the goddess's whole chthonic stratum. Her attestation is manuscript evidence: the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál), the fourteenth-century AM 748 I 4to that alone preserves Baldrs draumar, and the early codices of Snorri's Edda, composed about 1220. The word beneath her is far better attested than the goddess: Gothic halja appears in Ulfilas's fourth-century Bible translation, and Old English helle and Old High German hella fill the continental record as the name of the dead's place — but nowhere outside Scandinavia does the place carry a person. That distribution is itself the central datum for the scholarly debate over whether Hel the goddess is an old figure or a late personification of the grave-word, a question Simek and Lindow keep open. Saxo's Proserpina in Gesta Danorum Book 1 is the nearest thing to an independent witness: a Danish historian, a generation before Snorri's Edda reached its final form, already translating her for Latin readers.
